The fish sees the bird **raised**, its height multiplied by **n**, and adds its own
depth unchanged.
**Step 1 — treat the bird's height.** Looking from water up into air, the fish sees the
bird's apparent height as
**ny** ✓
since for an observer in the **denser** medium the object in the rarer one appears
**further away** by the factor n.
**Step 2 — treat the fish's own depth.** The fish is **in** the water, so its own
distance to the surface, **x**, is unaffected by any refraction ✓
**Step 3 — add.**
apparent distance = **x + ny** ✓
**Why the bird appears higher, not lower.** Rays from the bird bend **towards the
normal** as they enter the water ✓ Projected back by the fish, they meet above the
bird's true position - so the bird seems further up than it is.
**The rule, stated carefully.**
observer in the **rarer** medium looking into the **denser**: the object appears
**nearer**, by the factor **1/n** ✓ - this is ordinary apparent depth
observer in the **denser** medium looking into the **rarer**: the object appears
**further**, by the factor **n** ✓ - the case here
The two are reciprocal, which is why the formula apparent = real x n appears rather
than real/n.
**A numerical instance.** A bird 3 m up, a fish 1 m down, with n = 4/3:
apparent height of bird = (4/3)(3) = **4 m**
total apparent distance = 1 + 4 = **5 m** ✓ against the true 4 m.
**The companion question.** To the **bird**, the fish appears **nearer** the surface:
apparent distance = y + x/n ✓ which is a different expression entirely - and the fourth
option, offered to catch anyone who confuses the two viewpoints.
**Why the fish's own depth is not scaled.** No refraction occurs between the fish and
the surface - both are in the same medium ✓ Only light crossing the boundary is bent.
**Snell's window, for context.** The fish's entire view of the sky is compressed into a
cone of half-angle **48·8°** ✓ Within it the world above appears, distorted and raised;
outside it the fish sees only the reflected pond bottom.
**Reading the distractors.** **x + y(1 ± 1/n)** ✗ apply the apparent-depth factor to
the wrong quantity and in the wrong direction. **y + x(1 − 1/n)** ✗ swaps the roles of
the two media entirely ✓
∴ x + ny.

**Tourmaline** is the classic **dichroic** crystal.
**Step 1 — define dichroism.** A dichroic crystal **absorbs** one plane of polarisation
far more strongly than the perpendicular one ✓ Unpolarised light entering it emerges
**plane-polarised**, because one component has been selectively removed.
**Step 2 — identify the example.** **Tourmaline** does exactly this ✓ A plate cut
parallel to its optic axis transmits the component vibrating parallel to the axis and
absorbs the perpendicular one almost completely.
**The classic experiment.** Two tourmaline plates in series ✓ With their axes
**parallel**, light passes; rotate one through **90°** and the light is **extinguished**.
That demonstration, performed since the early nineteenth century, is the standard proof
that light is a **transverse** wave.
**Why dichroism proves transversality.** A **longitudinal** wave - sound, for instance -
has no plane of vibration to select ✓ Only a transverse wave can be polarised, so the
effect could not exist for sound.
**The modern descendant.** **Polaroid** sheet, invented by Edwin Land in 1929 ✓ Long
chains of polyvinyl alcohol are stretched and doped with iodine, absorbing the
component along the chains - synthetic dichroism, cheap and in large sheets. It is in
every pair of polarising sunglasses.
**Why the other crystals are not dichroic.**
**quartz** ✗ - **birefringent** and optically **active**; it splits a ray into two and
rotates the plane of polarisation, but absorbs neither component
**mica** ✗ - birefringent, and used for **quarter-wave** and **half-wave plates**, which
change the **state** of polarisation without absorbing
**selenite** ✗ - a form of gypsum, also birefringent ✓
All three are doubly refracting, but none **absorbs** one component.
**The distinction worth keeping.**
**birefringence** - **splits** light into two rays travelling at different speeds ✓
**dichroism** - **absorbs** one of them ✓
Tourmaline is both, but it is the absorption that makes it a polariser.
**Malus's law, which governs the second plate.**
I = I₀cos²θ ✓ giving full transmission at θ = 0 and complete extinction at 90°.
∴ Tourmaline.

Contact lets the charges **share equally**, so compare the products before and after.
**Step 1 — write the force before contact.**
F ∝ q₁q₂ = (12)(8) = **96** ✓ in units of µC², and the force is **attractive**, the
charges being opposite.
**Step 2 — find the charges after contact.** Identical spheres share the **total**
charge equally:
total = +12 − 8 = **+4 µC**
each = **+2 µC** ✓
**Step 3 — write the force after.**
F′ ∝ (2)(2) = **4** ✓ now **repulsive**, both being positive.
**Step 4 — take the ratio.**
F/F′ = 96/4
= **24 : 1** ✓
**Why the charges share equally.** The spheres are **identical**, so by symmetry they
must end at the same potential with the same charge ✓ Unequal spheres would share in
proportion to their radii.
**Why the force collapses so much.** Partial **neutralisation** ✓ The +12 and −8
largely cancel, leaving only +4 to be divided. The product falls from 96 to 4 - a
factor of 24 - even though the total charge magnitude fell only from 20 to 4.
**The sign change.** Before contact the force is **attractive**; after, **repulsive** ✓
The question asks only for the ratio of magnitudes, but the reversal is the more
striking physical change.
**The general result.** For charges q₁ and q₂ brought into contact and separated,
F′/F = [(q₁ + q₂)/2]²/(q₁q₂) ✓
Here (4/2)²/96 = 4/96 = 1/24 ✓
**When the force would vanish entirely.** If the charges were **equal and opposite** ✓
They would neutralise completely and no force would remain - F′/F = 0.
**When contact would make no difference.** If the charges were already **equal** ✓ Then
each keeps what it had and the force is unchanged.
**Why the distance drops out.** It is the same before and after, so r² cancels in the
ratio ✓ The whole answer lies in the product of the charges.
**A note on the question's units.** It writes **µF** where it plainly means **µC** ✓
Capacitance has no place in a Coulomb's-law problem, and the options confirm that
charges are intended.
**Reading the distractors.** **12 : 1**, **8 : 1** and **4 : 1** ✗ are the individual
charge magnitudes read as ratios ✓ Only the **product** 96 : 4 gives 24 : 1.
∴ 24 : 1.

Series connection raises the **voltage** rating; parallel raises the **capacitance** -
so a grid of both is needed.
**Step 1 — meet the voltage requirement.** Each capacitor withstands **200 V**, and
600 V is needed:
600/200 = **3 in series** ✓
**Step 2 — find that row's capacitance.** Three 6 µF capacitors in series:
C = 6/3 = **2 µF** ✓
**Step 3 — meet the capacitance requirement.** Rows of 2 µF in parallel must total
18 µF:
18/2 = **9 rows** ✓
**Step 4 — count the capacitors.**
3 x 9 = **27** ✓
**Why series raises the voltage rating.** The applied voltage divides equally between
identical capacitors in series ✓ Three in series across 600 V put only **200 V** across
each - exactly at the limit.
**Why parallel raises the capacitance.** Parallel capacitances **add** ✓ while all
share the same voltage. Nine rows of 2 µF give 18 µF, with 600 V across every row.
**The general recipe.**
rows in **series**: n = V_required/V_rating ✓
rows in **parallel**: m = C_required/(C_single/n) ✓
total = **mn** capacitors.
**A check on the arrangement.** Each capacitor carries 200 V and the grid stores
Q = CV = 18 µF x 600 V = **10·8 mC** ✓
Each of the 9 rows carries 1·2 mC, and within a row all three capacitors carry that
same 1·2 mC - consistent with series behaviour.
**Why a different split will not do.** Fewer than three in series and the capacitors
are **over-volted** and will break down ✓ More than three wastes capacitance
unnecessarily.
**The energy stored.**
U = ½CV² = ½(18 x 10⁻⁶)(600)² = **3·24 J** ✓ shared equally among the 27 units, 0·12 J
each.
**Why capacitors behave opposite to resistors.** Series capacitors **reduce** the total
and parallel ones **add** ✓ the reverse of the resistor rules, which is the usual
stumbling block in these problems.
**Reading the distractors.** **9** ✗ meets the capacitance only if the voltage rating
were already adequate. **18** ✗ and **3** ✗ satisfy one requirement but not both ✓ Both
conditions must be met simultaneously, and 27 is the smallest number that does.
∴ 27.

The solar spectrum is a **continuous** background crossed by dark **Fraunhofer**
lines - a **line absorption** spectrum.
**Step 1 — identify the source of the continuum.** The Sun's **photosphere** is hot and
dense, so it radiates a **continuous** spectrum ✓ approximately that of a black body at
5800 K.
**Step 2 — identify what absorbs.** The cooler gases of the **chromosphere** and the
Sun's outer atmosphere lie above it ✓ Each element absorbs at precisely the wavelengths
it would emit, removing narrow slices from the continuum.
**Step 3 — conclude.** Dark lines on a bright continuous background - a **line
absorption** spectrum ✓
**The Fraunhofer lines.** Catalogued in 1814, and labelled A, B, C, D … ✓ The
prominent **D lines** at 589 nm are **sodium**; the **H and K** lines are **calcium**;
and the **C and F** lines are hydrogen's H_α and H_β.
**Why the dark lines are not truly black.** The absorbing layer also **re-emits** - but
in all directions ✓ so only a fraction travels towards us, and the line appears dark
rather than empty.
**What the lines reveal.** The Sun's **composition**, measured element by element ✓
This is how helium was discovered in 1868, and how we know the Sun is 71% hydrogen and
27% helium without ever visiting it.
**Kirchhoff's law behind it all.** A gas absorbs exactly the wavelengths it emits ✓
Seen **against** the bright photosphere the chromosphere's lines are **dark**; seen at
the edge during a total eclipse, against the dark sky, the very same lines appear
**bright** - the flash spectrum.
**What else the lines tell us.** Their **Doppler shifts** give radial velocities and so
reveal binary stars, exoplanets and the expansion of the universe ✓ Their **Zeeman
splitting** measures magnetic fields, and their **widths** give pressures and
temperatures.
**Why not a band spectrum.** Bands come from **molecules**, which are mostly dissociated
at the Sun's temperature ✓ Some molecular bands do appear in cool sunspots and in
cooler stars, but the solar spectrum proper is atomic.
**Reading the distractors.** **Continuous emission** ✗ describes the photosphere alone,
ignoring the lines - which are the whole point. **Line emission** ✗ is the eclipse
flash spectrum. **Band absorption** ✗ needs molecules ✓
∴ line absorption spectrum.

The **minimum** wavelength of a series is its **series limit**, from n = ∞.
**Step 1 — write the Lyman limit.** The shortest wavelength comes from the largest
energy drop, n = ∞ → 1:
1/λ_L = R(1/1² − 0) = **R**
**λ_L = 1/R** ✓
**Step 2 — write the Balmer limit.** From n = ∞ → 2:
1/λ_B = R(1/2² − 0) = **R/4**
**λ_B = 4/R** ✓
**Step 3 — take the ratio.**
λ_L/λ_B = (1/R)/(4/R)
= 1/4
= **0·25** ✓
**The actual wavelengths.** With R = 1·097 x 10⁷ m⁻¹:
Lyman limit: **91·2 nm** ✓ far ultraviolet
Balmer limit: **364·6 nm** ✓ just beyond the violet
and their ratio is exactly **0·25** ✓
**Why the Lyman series is so much more energetic.** It ends on **n = 1**, the most
tightly bound level ✓ The full 13·6 eV is released at the series limit, against only
3·4 eV for Balmer - a factor of four in energy, hence a factor of four in wavelength.
**What the series limit means physically.** The electron falls from a **free** state,
just barely unbound, into the final level ✓ So the limit wavelength corresponds exactly
to the **ionisation energy** from that level:
Lyman limit: 1240/91·2 = **13·6 eV** ✓
Balmer limit: 1240/364·6 = **3·4 eV** ✓
**Beyond the limit.** A **continuum** ✓ Electrons arriving with kinetic energy to spare
produce a smooth spectrum beyond the series edge, not discrete lines.
**The general formula for any series limit.**
λ_min = **n₁²/R** ✓
so Lyman gives 1/R, Balmer 4/R, Paschen 9/R - the squares of the final quantum number.
**Why 0·25 and not 4.** The question asks for **Lyman to Balmer** ✓ and Lyman's
wavelength is the **shorter**, so the ratio is less than one. Reversing them gives 4,
which is a natural slip.
**Reading the distractors.** **1·25** ✗ and **0·5** ✗ correspond to no pair of series
limits. **4** ✗ is the reciprocal ✓ The ratio of the squares of the final quantum
numbers, 1² : 2², settles it.
∴ 0.25.

Count the alphas from the **mass number** and the betas from the **atomic number**.
**Step 1 — use the mass number to find the alphas.** Only alpha decay changes A, by 4
each time:
ΔA = 235 − 203 = **32**
number of alphas = 32/4 = **8** ✓
**Step 2 — find the atomic number after those alphas.** Each alpha lowers Z by 2:
92 − 8(2) = 92 − 16 = **76** ✓
**Step 3 — use the betas to make up the difference.** The final Z is 82, and each beta
**raises** Z by 1:
82 − 76 = **6 betas** ✓
**Step 4 — state the answer.** **α = 8, β = 6** ✓
**Step 5 — verify both bookkeepings.**
mass number: 235 − 8(4) − 6(0) = 235 − 32 = **203** ✓
atomic number: 92 − 8(2) + 6(1) = 92 − 16 + 6 = **82** ✓ both correct.
**Why alphas must be counted first.** Only alpha decay changes **A** ✓ so the mass
number fixes their number unambiguously, with no interference from the betas. The betas
then adjust Z.
**Why the order of the decays does not matter.** The changes in A and Z simply **add** ✓
Fourteen decays in any sequence give the same final nuclide.
**The general formulas.**
number of α = **(A_parent − A_daughter)/4** ✓
number of β = **2(number of α) − (Z_parent − Z_daughter)** ✓
Here 2(8) − 10 = **6** ✓
**Why alpha and beta alternate in nature.** Alpha decay removes two protons and two
neutrons, pushing the daughter **neutron-rich** relative to the line of stability ✓ Beta
decay then converts a neutron to a proton and restores the balance - which is why the
natural decay chains are long α-β sequences.
**A note on this particular chain.** ²³⁵U heads the **actinium series**, which in
reality ends at **²⁰⁷Pb** after 7 alphas and 4 betas ✓ The question's ²⁰³Pb is a
constructed example; the method is what matters.
**Reading the distractors.** **α = 6** ✗ would leave A = 211, not 203 - the mass number
settles the alphas immediately. **α = 3** ✗ is further out, and **α = 6, β = 0** ✗
fails on both counts ✓
∴ α = 8, β = 6.

The **proton** is the only baryon that is stable.
**Step 1 — recall what a baryon is.** A hadron made of **three quarks** ✓ The proton
(uud) and neutron (udd) are the lightest; the lambda, sigma, xi and omega are heavier.
**Step 2 — compare their lifetimes.**
**proton**: no decay has ever been observed ✓ experiment sets a lower limit of over
**10³⁴ years** - some 10²⁴ times the age of the universe
**neutron**: free, it decays with a half-life of about **10·2 minutes** ✓
**lambda**: **2·6 x 10⁻¹⁰ s**
**omega**: **8·2 x 10⁻¹¹ s** ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** The **proton** is the most stable - effectively absolutely so ✓
**Why the proton cannot decay.** It is the **lightest** baryon ✓ and **baryon number**
is conserved in every observed interaction, so there is no lighter baryon for it to
decay into. Conservation of energy and of baryon number together protect it.
**Why the neutron can.** It is slightly **heavier** than the proton - by 1·3 MeV - so
n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ is energetically allowed ✓ and the weak interaction permits it.
**Why the neutron survives inside a nucleus.** The binding energy makes the decay
energetically **forbidden** in most nuclei ✓ which is why ordinary matter is stable even
though free neutrons are not.
**Why anyone looks for proton decay.** Grand unified theories predict a lifetime of
10³¹ to 10³⁶ years ✓ Enormous detectors - Super-Kamiokande watches 50 000 tonnes of
water - have searched for decades and seen nothing, ruling out the simplest of those
theories.
**Why the proton's stability matters.** All ordinary matter is built on it ✓ If the
proton decayed at any appreciable rate, atoms, stars and we ourselves would dissolve.
**The classification, for context.**
**baryons**: three quarks - proton, neutron, lambda, omega ✓
**mesons**: quark-antiquark - pion, kaon ✓
**leptons**: fundamental, no quarks - electron, muon, neutrinos ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **Neutron** ✗ lives only minutes when free. **Omega** ✗ and
**lambda** ✗ decay in fractions of a nanosecond ✓
∴ proton.
